method: Visible original Codes-Xlsx and SysCheck dialogs. Source/target picker cancellations, actual saves and post-crash restarts executed through native UI. Input bytes pushed and read back before opening. Export files pulled after the native command returned.
comparison: All Excel sheet names, dimensions and cell text values. Code exports additionally validate per-column counts, alternating alphabet and uniqueness before normalizing random draws. CSV exports compared without value normalization.
product: 24 cases: comma/semicolon × UTF-8/UTF-16LE-BOM/Windows-1252 × normal/escaped-quotes/multiline/unquoted. UTF-8 BOM, UTF-16BE BOM, two ragged-row cases, UTF-32LE/BE BOM and a valid recovery input add seven successful cases. Two deliberately invalid files expose original crashes.
correction: Explicit Windows SysCheck CSV mode reproduces File.ReadAllLines BOM decoding/default UTF-8 replacement and the original per-line quote-delimiter splitting. The existing extended CSV mode remains default and preserves proper CSV semantics.
qualifiedDifferences: SC28: original crashes in String.Substring on a line shorter than two characters. Browser rejects it in the current form.
SC29: original crashes in ToXlsx for an empty file and leaves a partial workbook. Browser rejects it without offering a partial export. SC32 proves native recovery after restarting.
scopeNotes: Codes generator has no command to reopen its own output; saved XLSX files are parsed and compared, not claimed opened in a nonexistent native command.
Native OS file-dialog cancellations are captured. Browser download-dialog behavior remains controlled by each browser.
An initial forward-slash absolute filename attempt was rejected by the Windows file dialog; final Codes path selected through actual folders. That attempt is not an export pair.
A guest-file pull returning zero bytes was not treated as proof of file existence; captured exports require ZIP signature, checksum and successful workbook parsing.
limits: Synthetic files only; no empirical study data.
No universal equivalence of arbitrary malformed CSV encodings or Excel visual rendering.
Known original crashes are documented, not reproduced in the browser.
